Forensic Reserve: Eliciting Latent Knowledge for Image Forgery Detection

Find a pretrained model’s latent forensic reserve, then constrain lightweight adaptation to those existing directions.

Li Jiahua·John Zixu·Zhong Tom·Wu Fuping·Xu Tianhao·Zheng Jianqing·Mo Yuanhan·Shen Fei

October 6, 2026 ·Preprint ·Read the paper ·PDF
1Why this matters 2How it works 3What the study finds 4What this means

The short version

Reserve-Guided Elicitation translates the localization of sparse, origin-sensitive components into structural constraints for adapters. The goal is to strengthen existing forensic responses with a small adaptation budget.

500Labelled training images
<0.2%Trainable parameter budget
8Pretrained encoders

Why this matters

A pretrained representation may already contain useful forensic signals that ordinary task adaptation does not specifically exploit. Identifying where those signals reside can guide which components should be adapted.

How it works

  1. Use F-lens to decompose activations and screen components by real-versus-generated response differences.
  2. Map selected directions back to hidden-state space and place Forensic Reserve Adapters at identified sites.
  3. Train only coefficient maps; keep the backbone, fitted reference classifier, and subspace bases fixed.

What the study finds

With 500 labelled images and fewer than 0.2% trainable backbone parameters, RGE is evaluated on three benchmarks without target-benchmark adaptation. Improvements over corresponding frozen detectors hold across eight encoders.

What this means

Localization becomes operational when it constrains the adaptation itself: where to update, along which directions, and with how many parameters.
